prompt: Why does the lesson call uploading a file to a public analysis service publishing it?

choices.text: Because the service posts every file on social media
choices.why: Nothing so dramatic; the sharing is with its customers and partners.

choices.text: The service keeps and shares it
choices.why: Right: VirusTotal's premium customers can download it.

choices.text: Because the upload travels without encryption
choices.why: The upload is over HTTPS; the sharing happens afterwards.

choices.text: Because the file's author is notified
choices.why: Nobody is notified; the file is kept.

prompt: A colleague wants to upload a client's spreadsheet to VirusTotal "to check it". What is the problem?

choices.text: Spreadsheets cannot carry anything harmful, so it is a waste of time
choices.why: They can carry macros; the problem is elsewhere.

choices.text: VirusTotal refuses spreadsheets larger than a few pages
choices.why: Size is not the issue.

choices.text: It leaks the client's data, and the firm answers for it
choices.why: Right, under the LGPD; it goes to private analysis instead.

choices.text: The detection ratio would be meaningless for an office file
choices.why: It would mean as much as for any file; the leak is the problem.

prompt: Put the lesson's triage steps in order.
items: decide whether it may be uploaded
write down the hash, where, what and when

prompt: How did `file` know that fatura-outubro.pdf is a shell script?

choices.text: From the .pdf extension
choices.why: The extension said PDF; file disagreed.

choices.text: From its first bytes, #! instead of %PDF
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: By running it in a sandbox
choices.why: Nothing was run.

choices.text: By looking its hash up online
choices.why: The lab has no internet; file reads the content.

prompt: Why is the SHA-256 hash the right thing to search for and record?

choices.text: Because it compresses the file so it can be sent faster
choices.why: A hash cannot be turned back into the file.

choices.text: Because it proves the file is safe when no engine knows it
choices.why: An unknown hash proves nothing about safety.

choices.text: It names the file exactly, and reveals nothing more
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Because two different files always share the same hash
choices.why: The opposite: one changed byte changes it completely.

prompt: How many hexadecimal characters does a SHA-256 hash have?
What did `strings` reveal about the sample that a defender can use right away?

choices.text: A web address to block and look up
choices.why: Right: the domain goes to lesson 14's resolver.

choices.text: The name of the person who wrote it
choices.why: No author is in it.

choices.text: A password used by the script to log in somewhere
choices.why: There is none; there is an address.

choices.text: Proof that it already ran on desk
choices.why: strings reads the file; it says nothing about running.

prompt: In the YARA rule, the condition `$shebang ___ 0` requires the script mark to be the very first bytes of the file.
What does a YARA rule written from one sample give the firm?

choices.text: A copy of the sample, stored safely
choices.why: The rule describes; it stores nothing.

choices.text: A guarantee that no similar file will ever arrive
choices.why: It detects; it does not prevent arrival.

choices.text: A score from several dozen engines
choices.why: That is VirusTotal.

choices.text: The next similar file is found without an analyst
choices.why: Right.

prompt: A hash lookup on VirusTotal finds nothing. What does that tell you?

choices.text: The file is safe, because dozens of engines would know it
choices.why: Engines know what they have seen; this has not been seen.

choices.text: Only that nobody has submitted this exact file to the service yet
choices.why: Right; a targeted file is new by definition.

choices.text: That the hash was typed wrong
choices.why: Possible, and not what the result means.

choices.text: That VirusTotal is down
choices.why: A down service would not answer at all.

prompt: Your own signed installer gets 2 detections out of 70. What is the best reading?

choices.text: Malware: any detection means the file is infected
choices.why: Heuristic engines flag installers; lesson 7 called these false positives.

choices.text: Clean: 68 engines said nothing, so the 2 are wrong
choices.why: A few engines can be the first to see something new.

choices.text: Evidence to read: which engines, what they call it, and when
choices.why: Right: the ratio is evidence, not a verdict.

choices.text: Ask VirusTotal to remove the file
choices.why: That changes nothing about what the engines saw.

prompt: The lesson shows a curl command for VirusTotal's API. What does it send?

choices.text: The whole file, encoded for the API
choices.why: It sends a hash in the address.

choices.text: A hash and an API key
choices.why: Right; and it was not run here.

choices.text: The strings found in the file
choices.why: Only the hash is in the request.

choices.text: The YARA rule, to be run on VirusTotal's side
choices.why: That is a different, paid feature, not this command.

prompt: Which urlscan visibility leaks most, and is the default for anonymous use?

choices.text: Public
choices.why: Right: listed on the front page and in search.

choices.text: Unlisted
choices.why: Visible with the link and to paying customers, not to everybody.

choices.text: Private
choices.why: Only the submitting account sees it.

choices.text: Encrypted
choices.why: urlscan has no such setting.

prompt: Why should a password-reset link never be scanned on urlscan, even privately?

choices.text: Because urlscan cannot open pages that ask for a password
choices.why: It opens the page; that is the danger.

choices.text: It uses up a one-time token
choices.why: Right, and a public scan also hands it to strangers.

choices.text: Because reset links are always malicious
choices.why: Most are genuine; that is why scanning them hurts.

choices.text: Because private scans are shared with partners anyway
choices.why: Private scans are visible only to the account.

prompt: Which parts of a urlscan report does the lesson tell you to read? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: the final address after redirects
choices.why: Where the link really leads.

choices.text: the domains contacted
choices.why: Candidates for lesson 14's list.

choices.text: the screenshot
choices.why: What a person would have seen.

choices.text: the detection ratio of the page's images
choices.why: That is not part of a urlscan report.

prompt: An online sandbox reports that a document did nothing. Why is that weaker than "the document is harmless"?

choices.text: Because sandboxes only run documents, never scripts
choices.why: They run both.

choices.text: Because the report is only shown to paying customers
choices.why: Free reports are public, which is a different problem.

choices.text: Some samples wait, or detect the virtual machine
choices.why: Right: clean means nothing ran there.

choices.text: Because sandboxes have no network
choices.why: They record network activity.

prompt: Match each part of a sandbox report with where a defender takes it.
What sets any.run apart from Joe Sandbox, as the lesson describes them?

choices.text: any.run keeps every report private by default
choices.why: Its free plan makes analyses public.

choices.text: The analyst clicks inside the running machine
choices.why: Right: it is interactive.

choices.text: any.run only analyses links
choices.why: It runs files.

choices.text: any.run runs on the student's own computer
choices.why: That is lesson 12's sandbox.

prompt: What does RDAP add over WHOIS?

choices.text: It reveals the owner even when the record is redacted
choices.why: Redaction applies to both.

choices.text: Structured JSON over HTTPS, the same for every registry
choices.why: Right, instead of free text per registry.

choices.text: A reputation score for each domain
choices.why: RDAP holds registration data, not reputation.

choices.text: Faster resolution of the domain's address
choices.why: That is DNS, not registration data.

prompt: A domain sending payment slips to Jatobá's clients was created nine days ago. How does the lesson weigh that?

choices.text: As proof: new domains are always malicious
choices.why: New honest businesses register domains every day.

choices.text: As irrelevant, since age says nothing about intent
choices.why: It is one of the strongest single signals.

choices.text: As a strong signal, read with resemblance and behaviour
choices.why: Right: together they support lesson 14's decision.

choices.text: As a reason to report the registrar to the police
choices.why: The registrar did nothing wrong by registering it.

prompt: A partner firm emails an unexpected .zip. Under the lesson's order, what happens before anything goes online?

choices.text: file, the hash, strings and YARA, on your own machine
choices.why: Right; then the hash is searched.

choices.text: Upload to VirusTotal, because a partner's file is not the firm's
choices.why: It may carry the partner's own data; and the hash comes first anyway.

choices.text: Open it in the mail client's preview to see what it is
choices.why: Opening is what the order avoids.

choices.text: Run it in an online sandbox
choices.why: That publishes it; it comes last, if at all.
